searchnet: Network-Embedded Strategic Search Simulation in R

Manuscript prepared for the Journal of Statistical Software. searchnet 0.12.2.

Stephen Downing, University of Missouri

Abstract

The NK fitness landscape model is among the most widely used computational frameworks in strategy and organization theory, yet it treats the complexity parameter \(K\) as exogenous, the landscape as fixed, and agents as isolated searchers. The R package searchnet addresses all three limitations by reformulating the NK model as a bipartite network of \(M\) actors affiliating with \(N\) components and embedding it within a Stochastic Actor-Oriented Model (SAOM). This reformulation reveals that the scalar \(K\) is a special case of a four-dimensional coupled degree system—Expansiveness (\(K_{AC}\)), Popularity (\(K_{CA}\)), Sociality (\(K_{AA}\)), and Epistasis (\(K_{CC}\))—whose dynamics are governed by actors’ forward-looking affiliation decisions rather than imposed by the modeler. The package provides an R6-based simulation engine built on RSiena, a clean functional API (saomnk_env, saomnk_model, saomnk_run), coupled degree visualization through the \(\{K\}\)-4 panel, utility decomposition diagnostics, exogenous shock infrastructure, and validation against the classical NK model. Worked illustrations demonstrate reproduction of classical NK search dynamics and quasi-experimental shock analysis. Benchmarks against raw RSiena quantify computational overhead and scalability. searchnet targets researchers in strategic management, organizational theory, innovation economics, and computational social science who study search, adaptation, and competitive dynamics on complex landscapes.

1 Introduction

The NK fitness landscape model (Kauffman and Levin 1987; Kauffman and Weinberger 1989) has become one of the most productive computational frameworks in strategic management and organization theory. Since Levinthal (1997) demonstrated that the NK model could illuminate the tension between exploration and exploitation on rugged performance landscapes, hundreds of studies have deployed it to investigate organizational adaptation, modular design, imitation, and competitive search (Baumann et al. 2019; Rivkin 2000; Siggelkow and Rivkin 2005).

The model’s appeal lies in its parsimony. Two parameters—\(N\), the number of design choices or components, and \(K\), the degree of epistatic interdependence among them—generate landscapes ranging from smooth single-peaked surfaces (\(K = 0\)) to highly rugged terrains (\(K = N - 1\)) populated by many local optima. This parsimony has also become the model’s principal liability. Four limitations recur across the literature.

First, the fitness landscape is exogenous: it is drawn once from a random distribution and does not respond to the positions that agents occupy. Firms competing on the same landscape experience identical payoff surfaces regardless of how many competitors share each component or how concentrated competitive attention has become. Second, \(K\) is a scalar set by the modeler. In empirical organizational settings, interdependence is neither uniform nor fixed; some components are tightly coupled while others operate nearly independently, and coupling structures change as actors reconfigure their systems. Third, multi-agent extensions typically treat agents as independent searchers navigating the same landscape, ignoring the social and competitive structure through which firms observe, imitate, and crowd one another. Fourth, the NK model provides no statistical framework for parameter estimation from empirical data, making it difficult to discipline simulations with observed organizational behavior.

This paper introduces searchnet, an R package that addresses all four limitations simultaneously. The package reformulates the NK model as a bipartite network of \(M\) actors (firms, agents, decision-makers) affiliating with \(N\) components (technologies, resources, markets, design choices). By embedding this bipartite structure within a Stochastic Actor-Oriented Model (SAOM; Snijders 1996; Snijders et al. 2010), the search environment becomes a network data generation process whose topology—and therefore whose fitness landscape—co-evolves with actors’ affiliation decisions (Figure 1).

The package provides an R6-based simulation engine, a functional user API that abstracts away RSiena’s internal naming conventions, comprehensive visualization through the \(\{K\}\)-4 panel and 3D phase space, utility decomposition diagnostics, exogenous shock infrastructure for quasi-experimental designs, multi-wave Monte Carlo facilities, specification robustness tools, an interactive strategy game mode, and a classroom teaching module. Thirteen vignettes accompany the package: a quick-start introduction, theoretical foundations, a full simulation walkthrough with strategies and shocks, a computational experiment design guide, a causal inference tutorial, an NK validation guide, a Blume–Gibbs convergence tutorial, basin geometry, the Brock–Durlauf economic foundation, empirical calibration, the proof chain, formal verification with Lean 4, and a Professional Development Workshop curriculum.

2 Models

2.1 The NK fitness landscape

The NK model (Kauffman and Levin 1987; Kauffman and Weinberger 1989) characterizes performance landscapes with two parameters. A system of \(N\) binary components (loci, design choices, technologies) generates \(2^N\) possible configurations. Each component \(d\) makes a fitness contribution \(f_d\) that depends not only on its own state but also on the states of \(K\) other components with which it is epistatically linked. Total fitness is the average contribution across all \(N\) components. When \(K = 0\), each component contributes independently and the landscape has a single global peak. As \(K\) increases toward \(N - 1\), the landscape becomes increasingly rugged, populated by exponentially many local optima that trap myopic searchers.

Levinthal (1997) introduced the NK model to management as a formalization of the exploration–exploitation trade-off: agents that search locally (single-bit mutations) on rugged landscapes quickly find nearby peaks but rarely discover the global optimum, while agents that search more broadly (multi-bit jumps) sacrifice short-run performance for a chance at higher peaks. This insight has been extended to organizational design (Siggelkow and Rivkin 2005), imitation (Rivkin 2000), modular architectures (Ethiraj and Levinthal 2004), and competitive interaction (Lenox et al. 2006).

2.2 Stochastic Actor-Oriented Models

Stochastic Actor-Oriented Models (Snijders 1996; Snijders et al. 2010) provide a continuous-time Markov model for the co-evolution of social networks and behavior. At each micro-step, a single actor is selected according to a rate function, evaluates the marginal utility of each possible tie change according to an objective function, and chooses probabilistically via a multinomial logit rule. The objective function takes the general form

\[\begin{equation} \label{eq:saom-objective} f_i(\mathbf{B}) = \sum_k \theta_k \, s_{ik}(\mathbf{B}), \end{equation}\]

where \(s_{ik}(\mathbf{B})\) are network statistics computed from the current network \(\mathbf{B}\) and \(\theta_k\) are parameters governing each actor’s preferences. The parameters \(\theta_k\) can be estimated from observed panel data using the method of moments or maximum likelihood, implemented in the RSiena package (Snijders et al. 2025).

SAOMs are well established in sociology and political science for modeling friendship networks, advice networks, and inter-organizational partnerships. They have been extended to bipartite (two-mode) networks (Koskinen and Edling 2012), where the model governs actors’ affiliation decisions with respect to events, organizations, or other categorical entities. searchnet exploits this bipartite extension to model actors affiliating with components in a search environment.

2.2.1 Why SAOM over ERGM?

A natural question is why searchnet adopts the SAOM rather than the exponential random graph model (ERGM; Lusher et al. 2012) or its temporal extension (TERGM; Hanneke et al. 2010) as its network engine. The choice follows directly from the theoretical premise of the NK tradition. ERGMs characterize the equilibrium distribution of network configurations without specifying a generative decision process. An ERGM answers the question “what network structures are over-represented relative to chance?” but does not model who makes which decision when. For a framework whose purpose is to endogenize landscape ruggedness through actors’ strategic choices, this equilibrium focus omits precisely the mechanism of interest.

2.3 The implemented model

Notation. Throughout this paper we adopt the following notation. The bipartite incidence matrix is \(\mathbf{B} \in \{0,1\}^{M \times N}\) with entries \(b_{ij}\); the NK configuration vector for a single agent is \(\mathbf{x} \in \{0,1\}^N\); the influence matrix is \(\mathbf{E}\) (implemented in RSiena as the weight matrix \(\mathbf{W}\) of the XWX effect); component payoff functions are \(f_d\); and the logit precision parameter is \(\beta > 0\).

A terminological note is warranted here, because the two ideas are routinely conflated. The matrix \(\mathbf{E}\) is an influence matrix in the sense of Rivkin and Siggelkow (2007): it states which components interact and with what sign, and it is an input supplied by the analyst. Epistasis is the consequence – the dependence of one component’s fitness contribution on the states of others, which arises when a portfolio is evaluated through \(\mathbf{E}\) as \(\sum_{j \neq h} x_j x_h e_{hj}\) (the XWX statistic). The distinction matters in searchnet because a third quantity sits between the two. The component-component degree \(K_{CC}\) records how far components are actually co-adopted at a given moment; it is computed from the realized affiliation matrix and does not read \(\mathbf{E}\), yet it evolves as a consequence of \(\mathbf{E}\), which drives the search that produces those affiliations. \(K_{CC}\) therefore indexes the coupling epistasis acts through, generally differs from the influence structure that generated it, and is not itself a measure of the fitness consequence. Accordingly the package argument is named influence_matrix; epistasis_matrix is retained as a deprecated alias.

2.3.1 Bipartite network formulation

The classical NK model represents a system configuration as an \(N\)-dimensional binary vector \(\mathbf{x} = (x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_N)\) where \(x_j \in \{0, 1\}\). searchnet generalizes this by introducing \(M\) actors, each of whom maintains an affiliation vector. The resulting system state is an \(M \times N\) binary matrix \(\mathbf{B}\), where \(b_{ij} = 1\) indicates that actor \(i\) affiliates with component \(j\). This matrix is the incidence matrix of a bipartite network with actor nodes on one side and component nodes on the other.

The bipartite representation has three immediate consequences. First, it naturally accommodates multiple agents searching simultaneously: each row of \(\mathbf{B}\) is an actor’s configuration, and actors’ configurations interact through shared columns. Second, it makes the search environment endogenous: the pattern of affiliations determines which components are coupled (via shared actors) and which actors are competitors (via shared components). Third, it provides the structural substrate for the SAOM engine: \(\mathbf{B}\) becomes the dependent variable in an evolving bipartite network model.

2.3.2 The \(\{K\}\) interpretive framework

The bipartite incidence matrix \(\mathbf{B}\) generates four coupled degree statistics, each of which is individually a standard network measure but whose joint dynamics expose the mechanism through which micro-level search decisions produce macro-level landscape structure. Table 1 summarizes the four dimensions.

The \(\{K\}\) coupled degree framework. Each dimension is a standard network statistic.
Dimension Symbol Interpretation Network measure
Expansiveness \(K_{AC}\) Components per actor Bipartite row degree
Popularity \(K_{CA}\) Actors per component Bipartite column degree
Sociality \(K_{AA}\) Co-affiliating actors per actor Actor projection degree (distinct partners)
Epistasis \(K_{CC}\) Co-occurring components per component Component projection degree (distinct partners)

Table 2 translates the elements of the model into three business domains.

The elements of SAOM-NK in three business domains. Popularity is read only when a statistic distinguishes among holders, here by an actor attribute (reputation, certification, prestige).
Model element Technology portfolios Retail assortments Product design
Actor (row of \(\mathbf{B}\)) firm retail chain design team
Component (column of \(\mathbf{B}\)) technology class product category product module
Tie \(b_{ij} = 1\) firm patents in the class chain carries the category product includes the module
Influence matrix \(\mathbf{W}\) complementarity between classes cross-selling between categories interfaces between modules
Expansiveness (\(K_{AC}\)) breadth of the technology portfolio assortment breadth modules per product
Epistasis (\(K_{CC}\)) value of combining complementary classes basket value of co-carried categories fit of modules that share interfaces
Sociality (\(K_{AA}\)) technological overlap with rivals assortment overlap with competing chains modules shared across teams
Popularity (\(K_{CA}\)) classes held by high-reputation firms categories carried by certified chains modules used by prestigious products
Example effect (reads \(\rightarrow\) moves) outAct: Expansiveness \(\rightarrow\) Epistasis strength inPop: Sociality \(\rightarrow\) Sociality strength XWX: Epistasis \(\rightarrow\) Epistasis strength valued by \(\mathbf{W}\)

The classical NK parameter \(K\) is the W-degree: the number of other components with a nonzero entry in a component’s row of the influence matrix \(\mathbf{W}\). \(K_{CC}\), the degree in the component projection, counts the components co-held with it by at least one actor; the two coincide only when a component’s co-held partners are exactly its partners in \(\mathbf{W}\). In searchnet, \(\mathbf{W}\) is set by the modeler, while \(K_{CC}\) emerges from the bipartite network and co-evolves with the other three degree dimensions.

The analytical leverage of the \(\{K\}\) framework comes from treating these four measures as a coupled system rather than examining any one in isolation. Because all four derive from the same incidence matrix \(\mathbf{B}\), they are structurally linked. A change in Expansiveness (\(K_{AC}\)) mechanically alters Popularity (\(K_{CA}\)), which in turn reshapes both the actor co-membership network (\(K_{AA}\)) and the component co-occurrence network (\(K_{CC}\)). The projections are computed as:

\[\begin{align} \mathbf{P}_{AA} &= \mathbf{B} \mathbf{B}^\top - \text{diag}(\mathbf{B} \mathbf{B}^\top), \label{eq:proj-actor} \\ \mathbf{P}_{CC} &= \mathbf{B}^\top \mathbf{B} - \text{diag}(\mathbf{B}^\top \mathbf{B}). \label{eq:proj-component} \end{align}\]

The degree of actor \(i\) in the actor projection \(\mathbf{P}_{AA}\) is \(K_{AA,i} = \sum_{h \neq i} \mathbf{1}[(\mathbf{B}\mathbf{B}^\top)_{ih} > 0]\), and symmetrically for \(K_{CC,j}\) in the component projection. Analyzing any single measure in isolation obscures the cross-domain dependencies that link actor behavior to landscape topology.

The four statistics are individually well known in the bipartite network literature (Latapy et al. 2008; Borgatti and Everett 1997).

2.3.3 SAOM objective function specification

The SAOM objective function in searchnet governs actors’ affiliation decisions. At each micro-step, the selected actor \(i\) evaluates the change in objective function value for each possible tie change (creating or dissolving an affiliation with one component) and selects the change that maximizes expected utility, subject to a stochastic error term drawn from the type I extreme value distribution.

The objective function takes the form of Equation [eq:saom-objective], with the following key statistics:

\[\begin{equation} \label{eq:objective-classes} \begin{aligned} f_i(\mathbf{B}) ={}& \underbrace{\color{clsComplementarity}\textstyle\sum_{\ell}\theta^{(\ell)}_{\text{epist}} \sum_{j} b_{ij} \sum_{h \neq j} b_{ih}\, w^{(\ell)}_{hj}}_{ \substack{\text{\colorbox{clsComplementarity}{\textcolor{white}{\scriptsize\bfseries complementarity}}\ \colorbox{black}{\textcolor{white}{\scriptsize\bfseries $K_{CC}$}}}\\[1pt] \text{\scriptsize complementarity among held components}}} \;+\; \underbrace{\color{clsScope}\theta_{\text{dens}}\, b_{i+} + \theta_{\text{scope}}\, b_{i+}^{2}}_{ \substack{\text{\colorbox{clsScope}{\textcolor{white}{\scriptsize\bfseries scope}}\ \colorbox{black}{\textcolor{white}{\scriptsize\bfseries reads $K_{AC}$ $\mid$ moves $K_{CC}$}}}\\[1pt] \text{\scriptsize breadth of holdings}}} \\[4pt] &+\; \underbrace{\color{clsCrowding}\theta_{\text{pop}} \textstyle\sum_{j} b_{ij}\, b_{+j}}_{ \substack{\text{\colorbox{clsCrowding}{\textcolor{white}{\scriptsize\bfseries crowding}}\ \colorbox{black}{\textcolor{white}{\scriptsize\bfseries $K_{AA}$}}}\\[1pt] \text{\scriptsize crowding on, or pull toward, shared components}}} \;+\; \underbrace{\color{clsContact}\theta_{\text{close}}\, \tfrac{1}{2}\textstyle\sum_{h \neq i} \binom{o_{ih}}{2}}_{ \substack{\text{\colorbox{clsContact}{\textcolor{white}{\scriptsize\bfseries contact}}\ \colorbox{black}{\textcolor{white}{\scriptsize\bfseries reads $K_{AA}$ $\mid$ moves $K_{AA}$, $K_{CC}$}}}\\[1pt] \text{\scriptsize repeated overlap among actors}}} \\[4pt] &+\; \underbrace{\color{clsImitation}\theta_{\text{imit}} \textstyle\sum_{j} b_{ij}\, \bigl(\mathrm{sim}_{ij} - \overline{\mathrm{sim}}\bigr)}_{ \substack{\text{\colorbox{clsImitation}{\textcolor{white}{\scriptsize\bfseries imitation}}\ \colorbox{black}{\textcolor{white}{\scriptsize\bfseries reads $K_{CA}$ $\mid$ moves $K_{AA}$}}}\\[1pt] \text{\scriptsize attraction to components held by similar actors,}\\ \text{\scriptsize via covariate similarity (\texttt{simEgoInDist2})}}} \;+\; \underbrace{\color{clsCovariate}\theta_{\text{strat}}\, b_{i+}\tilde{v}_i + \theta_{\text{value}} \textstyle\sum_{j} b_{ij}\, \tilde{c}_j}_{ \substack{\text{\colorbox{clsCovariate}{\textcolor{white}{\scriptsize\bfseries covariates}}\ \colorbox{black}{\textcolor{white}{\scriptsize\bfseries reads $K_{AC}$ $\mid$ moves $K_{AC}$, $K_{CA}$}}}\\[1pt] \text{\scriptsize actor and component attributes}}} \end{aligned} \end{equation}\]

where \(b_{i+} = \sum_j b_{ij}\) is actor \(i\)’s degree, \(b_{+j} = \sum_h b_{hj}\) is component \(j\)’s degree (counting \(i\)), \(o_{ih} = \sum_j b_{ij} b_{hj}\) is the overlap of actors \(i\) and \(h\), \(\mathbf{W}^{(\ell)}\) is the \(\ell\)th influence matrix, \(\tilde{v}\) and \(\tilde{c}\) are actor and component covariates centered on their means (with centered = TRUE; the default, uncentered, statistic equals the centered one plus \(\bar{v}\, b_{i+}\) or \(\bar{c}\, b_{i+}\)), and \(\mathrm{sim}_{ij} = 1 - |v_i - \bar{v}_{-i,j}|/R_v\) compares \(v_i\) with the mean \(v\) of \(j\)’s other holders (\(R_v\) the range of \(v\); \(\bar{v}_{-i,j}\) is the mean of \(v\) when no other actor holds \(j\); \(\overline{\mathrm{sim}}\) the mean similarity over ordered pairs of distinct actors). Each term is the RSiena 1.5.0 two-mode statistic that searchnet computes; the co-holder performance similarity of saomnk_coholder_similarity() is a post hoc statistic and is not simulated.

SAOM objective function statistics in searchnet. Crowding reads as agglomeration when its coefficient is positive; the sign changes the reading, not the dimension. The two \(\{K\}\) columns are those of searchnet_effect_dimensions().
Construct RSiena name Statistic \(s_{ik}(\mathbf{B})\) \(\{K\}\) dimension read Moves (target statistic)
Scope (cost) density \(\sum_j b_{ij}\) Expansiveness total ties
Crowding inPop \(\sum_j b_{ij} \sum_{h} b_{hj}\) Sociality Sociality strength
Scope (breadth) outAct \(\bigl(\sum_j b_{ij}\bigr)^{2}\) Expansiveness Epistasis strength
Complementarity XWX \(\sum_j b_{ij} \sum_{h \neq j} b_{ih} w_{hj}\) Epistasis Epistasis strength valued by \(\mathbf{W}\)

The density effect serves as an intercept: a negative density parameter creates baseline sparsity pressure, preventing actors from affiliating with all components. The popularity effect (inPop) creates preferential attachment to components that many other actors already use. The scope effect (outAct) governs actors’ tendency to expand or contract the breadth of their affiliations. The epistasis effect (XWX) introduces exogenous component–component coupling via a modeler-supplied weight matrix \(\mathbf{W}\) (denoted \(\mathbf{E}\) in the formal proofs; see Section 6.1); actors derive utility from affiliating with components that are coupled to their existing affiliations.

Actor-level heterogeneity enters through constant covariates attached to the objective function. A covariate vector \(\mathbf{v}\) (e.g., encoding strategic orientation) can modify the weight an actor places on popularity seeking (inPopX), scope expansion (egoX), or component characteristics (altX). This mechanism allows the modeler to assign distinct strategic profiles to different actors—for example, “exploiters” who preferentially attach to popular components and “explorers” who expand into uncrowded niches.

The simulation proceeds via RSiena’s continuous-time Markov chain algorithm. Actors are selected according to a rate function (by default, equal rates for all actors), and the selected actor evaluates all possible single-tie changes, choosing according to a multinomial logit rule:

\[\begin{equation} \label{eq:choice} P(b_{ij} \to 1 - b_{ij}) = \frac{\exp\bigl(f_i(\mathbf{B}^{ij})\bigr)} {\sum_{j'=0}^{N} \exp\bigl(f_i(\mathbf{B}^{ij'})\bigr)}, \end{equation}\]

where \(\mathbf{B}^{ij}\) denotes the network configuration obtained by toggling actor \(i\)’s tie to component \(j\), and \(\mathbf{B}^{i0} = \mathbf{B}\) is the option to make no change. The search_rsiena method passes the full structure model to RSiena’s siena07 function, which executes the continuous-time simulation internally.

For exogenous shocks, searchnet partitions the simulation timeline into proportional segments. At each segment boundary, the \(\theta\) parameters are updated to new values specified by the shock schedule. The simulation then continues from the current network state with the modified objective function, preserving path dependence while allowing the researcher to model environmental discontinuities. This is equivalent to running sequential RSiena simulations where each wave’s initial state is the terminal state of the previous wave.

3 Software design

3.1 Architecture

searchnet is built on R6 classes organized in a two-level inheritance hierarchy:

SaomNkRSienaBiEnv_base

Core environment initialization, bipartite matrix management, graph construction, projection computation, and utility helpers (toggle, Jaccard, existence checks). This base class manages the \(M \times N\) incidence matrix, constructs the RSiena data objects, and provides low-level network operations.

SaomNkRSienaBiEnv

Full simulation engine inheriting from the base class, adding the search_rsiena() simulation method, chain statistics processing, \(\{K\}\)-4 degree computation, fitness landscape evaluation, shock handling, multi-wave experiment infrastructure, and the visualization interface.

Supporting modules provide separation of concerns:

  • saomnk-api.R: User-facing functional API (saomnk_env, saomnk_model, saomnk_run) that wraps the R6 internals.

  • nk-classic.R: A self-contained implementation of the classical NK model, used as an external reference for the reduction check of Section 5.1.

  • saomnk-experiments.R: SaoMNKexperiments R6 class for batch Monte Carlo simulation management.

  • plot-*.R: Ten modular plotting files (plot-utility.R, plot-degrees.R, plot-exploration.R, plot-markets.R, plot-multiwave.R, plot-shocks.R, plot-snapshots.R, plot-phase-space.R, plot-forbearance.R, plot-geo.R) containing visualization functions.

  • searchnet-game.R: Strategy game mode providing an interactive game loop where a human player controls one firm and competes against AI opponents that follow SAOM-NK logit choice rules.

  • searchnet-teaching.R: Classroom teaching module for Capsim-style strategy simulations supporting multiple industry presets, difficulty levels, and exogenous shocks.

  • utils.R: Standalone helper functions.

The package follows standard R packaging conventions with DESCRIPTION, NAMESPACE, a testthat test suite (820 tests across 65 files), and 14 vignettes. All exported functions are prefixed with saomnk_ or searchnet_ to avoid namespace collisions.

3.2 Simulation as state-carrying periods

A call to search_rsiena() simulates one unit of model time, not a fixed number of ministeps. Each block of identical parameter rows is run as one unconditional RSiena period, started from the end network of the previous block, so the path carries its state across shocks and waves. The argument iterations_per_actor (steps_per_actor in saomnk_run()) sets the basic rate, that is, the expected number of opportunities per actor at zero rate effects; the realized number of ministeps is random. The engine stops if replaying a segment’s chain does not end at RSiena’s own end network.

3.3 Guards

Four guards target failures that leave no trace in the output. Every effect declared in a model must appear as included in the fitted RSiena effects object, so a misspelled or unmatched effect stops the run instead of disappearing. Covariate centering is stated: monadic covariates are uncentered unless the model says otherwise, and the centering applied is recorded. Each run records its provenance, including segment seeds and the realized ministep count. Seeds are drawn from hashed, namespaced streams, so neighboring seeds share no segment seed.

3.4 Ecosystem

3.4.1 Manim animation pipeline

For presentation and pedagogical purposes, searchnet exports simulation data in formats compatible with the Manim animation library (Manim Community 2022). The exported data includes per-step bipartite matrices, projection networks, degree trajectories, and utility decompositions. This pipeline is accessed through the saomnk_export_manim() method on the environment object and the searchnet_export_phase_space() function for phase space data.

3.4.2 Interactive features

searchnet includes two interactive modules that extend the simulation engine from a research tool to an instructional platform. The searchnet_game_* family of functions (five exported functions) provides an interactive game loop where a human player controls one firm and competes against AI opponents that follow the SAOM conditional-logit choice rule. The searchnet_classroom_* family (six exported functions) supports Capsim-style strategy simulations for classroom use.

4 Using searchnet

4.1 User API

A central design goal of searchnet is to provide a clean functional interface that shields users from the complexity of RSiena’s internal naming conventions and the R6 class hierarchy. The workflow follows three steps: environment creation, model specification, and simulation execution.

4.1.1 Step 1: Create the search environment

The saomnk_env() function initializes a bipartite search environment:

R> env <- saomnk_env(M = 8, N = 12, density = 0, seed = 42)

This creates a SaomNkRSienaBiEnv object representing 8 actors and 12 components, starting from an empty network (all actors unaffiliated). The seed argument ensures reproducibility of the initial network draw.

4.1.2 Step 2: Specify the structure model

The saomnk_model() function builds the SAOM objective function specification using intuitive parameter names:

R> ## Define a modular influence matrix: 4 blocks of 3 components R> K_matrix <- saomnk_block_diagonal(12, 4) R> R> ## Specify the model R> mod <- saomnk_model( + density = -0.5, # sparsity pressure + popularity = 0.2, # preferential attachment + scope = 0.1, # scope expansion + influence_matrix = K_matrix, + influence_weight = 0.05 + ) R> mod

SaoMNK Structure Model ———————- Effects on the bipartite network DV (3): density (density) theta = -0.5 [fixed] crowding (inPop) theta = 0.2 [fixed] scope (outAct) theta = 0.1 [fixed] Influence / dyadic covariates (1): complementarity (XWX) theta = 0.05 [fixed] [influence matrix W, 12 x 12]

Users never need to write internal references such as "self$bipartite_rsienaDV" or construct nested covariate lists manually. The function assembles the complete RSiena structure model internally. Actor strategy heterogeneity is specified through the strategies argument:

R> ## Heterogeneous actors: varying scope and popularity preferences R> mod_strat <- saomnk_model( + density = -0.3, + popularity = 0.2, + scope = 0.1, + influence_matrix = K_matrix, + influence_weight = 0.05, + strategies = list( + egoX = rep(c(-1, 0, 1, 0), length.out = 8), + inPopX = rep(c( 1, 0,-1, 0), length.out = 8) + ) + )

4.1.3 Step 3: Run the simulation

The saomnk_run() function executes the SAOM simulation:

R> saomnk_run(env, mod, steps_per_actor = 30, seed = 12345)

The function passes the structure model to the internal search_rsiena() method, runs the continuous-time SAOM simulation via RSiena, extracts chain statistics, and computes the \(\{K\}\)-4 degree trajectories. The env object is modified in place (standard R6 semantics) and returned invisibly.

4.2 Mapping RSiena effects to strategic search concepts

The preceding objective function uses RSiena effect names that are standard in social network analysis but may be unfamiliar to strategy researchers. Table 4 provides a systematic mapping between RSiena effects available in searchnet and their strategic search interpretations. Each effect’s parameter symbol links it to the corresponding \(\{K\}\) dimension introduced in Section 2.3.2, enabling researchers to translate between the network estimation vocabulary and the strategy-theoretic language of scope, complementarity, and imitation.

Mapping RSiena effects to strategic search concepts. Parameters correspond to the SAOM objective function (Equation [eq:saom-objective]). The two \(\{K\}\) columns give the dimension each effect’s change statistic reads and the one its target statistic moves (searchnet_effect_dimensions()).
RSiena Effect Parameter \(\{K\}\) dimension read Moves (target statistic) Strategy Concept Interpretation
density \(\theta_{\text{dens}}\) Expansiveness total ties Scope cost Negative = costly to hold activities; controls portfolio breadth
outAct \(\theta_{\text{scope}}\) Expansiveness Epistasis strength Diminishing returns Quadratic penalty on actor degree (scope)
inPop \(\theta_{\text{pop}}\) Sociality Sociality strength Crowding / agglomeration Negative = avoid components other actors hold (crowding); positive = agglomeration
XWX \(\theta_{\text{epist}}\) Epistasis Epistasis strength valued by \(\mathbf{W}\) Complementarity / synergy Reward for holding epistatically linked components
simEgoInDist2 \(\theta_{\text{imit}}\) Popularity Sociality strength, similarity-weighted Imitation / herding Positive = prefer components held by covariate-similar actors (needs an actor covariate)
egoX \(\theta_{\text{strat}}\) Expansiveness Expansiveness, attribute-weighted Strategy heterogeneity Actor-level covariate modifying search behavior
altX \(\theta_{\text{value}}\) Expansiveness Popularity, attribute-weighted Component value Exogenous activity-level payoff differences
cycle4 \(\theta_{\text{close}}\) Sociality Sociality and Epistasis Contact Repeated overlap between pairs of actors (four-cycles)

The table makes explicit the division of labor among effects. The first four rows—density, outAct, inPop, and XWX—are the workhorses of most searchnet specifications. Together they endogenize the four \(\{K\}\) dimensions: scope cost sets the baseline, outAct introduces diminishing returns to breadth, inPop sets crowding on shared components (agglomeration when positive), and XWX rewards configurations that exploit exogenous complementarities. The remaining effects allow the researcher to layer on additional mechanisms: imitation (simEgoInDist2, which requires an actor covariate) draws actors toward components held by actors similar on that covariate, actor and component covariates (egoX, altX) introduce heterogeneity, and cycle4 captures repeated overlap between pairs of actors (contact). By selecting which effects to include and setting their parameter values, the researcher controls which strategic mechanisms are active in a given simulation—a design choice whose consequences can be audited with the diagnostic tools described in Section 5.1.

4.3 Visualization

searchnet provides a comprehensive visualization toolkit organized around four analytical perspectives.

4.3.1 The \(\{K\}\)-4 panel

The signature visualization is the coupled degree panel, which displays all four \(\{K\}\) dimensions over the simulation timeline:

R> saomnk_plot_k4(env, smooth = 0.3)

4.3.2 Network snapshots

The saomnk_plot_snapshots() function renders the bipartite network at selected simulation steps, along with its unipartite projections:

R> n_steps <- env\(get_step() R> saomnk_plot_snapshots(env, + steps = unique(pmax(1, round(c(0, 0.5, 1) * n_steps)))) \end{CodeInput} \begin{figure} {\centering \includegraphics{searchnet-jss_files/figure-latex/snapshots-1} } \caption[Network snapshots at the initial state, midpoint, and final state of the simulation]{Network snapshots at the initial state, midpoint, and final state of the simulation. In each snapshot, from left: the actor co-membership projection ($K_{AA}$), the bipartite actor-component network, and the component co-occurrence heatmap ($K_{CC}$).}\label{fig:snapshots-4} \end{figure} \end{CodeChunk} \subsubsection{Utility decomposition}\label{utility-decomposition} The \texttt{saomnk\_plot\_utility()} function decomposes each actor's total objective function value into contributions from individual network statistics: \begin{CodeChunk} \begin{CodeInput} R> saomnk_plot_utility(env, smooth = 0.35) \end{CodeInput} \begin{figure} {\centering \includegraphics{searchnet-jss_files/figure-latex/utility-1} } \caption[Utility decomposition showing each actor's objective function value broken into contributions from density, popularity, scope, and influence (\)W\() effects over the simulation timeline]{Utility decomposition showing each actor's objective function value broken into contributions from density, popularity, scope, and influence ($W$) effects over the simulation timeline.}\label{fig:utility} \end{figure} \end{CodeChunk} This decomposition provides direct insight into the strategic trade-offs governing search behavior: an actor whose utility is dominated by the epistasis term is searching for complementary components, while one dominated by the popularity term is following the crowd. \subsubsection{3D phase space}\label{d-phase-space} The \texttt{saomnk\_plot\_phase\_space\_3d()} function renders the simulation trajectory in a three-dimensional Network \(\times\) Behavior \(\times\) Fitness space, where the three axes correspond to structural properties (e.g., \(K_{AC}\) or density), behavioral properties (e.g., exploration rate or scope change), and outcome measures (utility or NK fitness). The resulting ``SCP(t) trajectory'\,' traces each actor's path through this space over simulation time, providing an integrated view of how structural position, behavioral strategy, and performance co-evolve. Supporting functions include \texttt{saomnk\_plot\_phase\_heatmap()} for density-based projections, \texttt{saomnk\_plot\_phase\_evolution()} for animated trajectories, \texttt{saomnk\_plot\_phase\_comparison()} for juxtaposing multiple simulation runs, and \texttt{searchnet\_export\_phase\_space()} for Manim-compatible data export. \subsection{Empirical calibration via SAOM parameter bridge}\label{sec:calibration} The \textbf{searchnet} package includes a calibration bridge that converts fitted SAOM parameters from empirical network panel data into calibrated SaoMNK simulation environments. This enables researchers to run validated counterfactual simulations using empirically grounded parameter estimates rather than ad hoc parameter choices. \subsubsection{Parameter mapping}\label{parameter-mapping} Both frameworks use the actor-oriented conditional logit utility \begin{equation}\label{eq:calibration-utility} U_i(x) = \sum_k \theta_k \, s_{ik}(x), \end{equation} where \(s_{ik}(x)\) is the network statistic for effect \(k\). The bridge maps \textbf{RSiena}'s \(\hat{\theta}\) vector to \textbf{searchnet}'s structure model effects. \texttt{.bridge\_crosswalk()} records each mapping as exact, approximate (refused when \texttt{strict = TRUE}) or unavailable: \begin{table}[ht] \centering \begin{tabular}{lll} \toprule \textbf{RSiena} effect & \textbf{searchnet} effect & Status \\ \midrule \texttt{density}, \texttt{inPop}, \texttt{inPopSqrt}, \texttt{outAct}, \texttt{outActSqrt} & same name & exact \\ \texttt{XWX}, \texttt{egoX}, \texttt{altX}, \texttt{X}, \texttt{totInDist2}, \texttt{simEgoInDist2} & same name & exact \\ \texttt{cycle3}, \texttt{recip} & \texttt{cycle4} & approximate (a different statistic) \\ \texttt{simX}, \texttt{sameX} & \texttt{egoX} & approximate (similarity read as a main effect) \\ \texttt{higher} & \texttt{altX} & approximate \\ \texttt{gwespFF}, \texttt{transTrip} & none & unavailable (one-mode only) \\ \bottomrule \end{tabular} \caption{Parameter mapping between RSiena and \textbf{searchnet}, from \texttt{.bridge\_crosswalk()}. Every mapped effect transforms as $\beta = \theta \cdot \alpha$, with $\alpha$ an optional scale factor applied during calibration.} \label{tab:param-mapping} \end{table} \subsubsection{Code example}\label{code-example} The calibration workflow involves three steps: parameter conversion, environment initialization from empirical data, and counterfactual execution. \begin{CodeChunk} \begin{CodeInput} R> ## Convert fitted SAOM parameters to SaoMNK R> bridge <- saom_to_saomnk(saom_fit, scale_factor = 1.0) R> print(bridge\)mapping_table) R> R> ## Initialize environment from empirical data R> env_data <- empirical_to_saomnk_env(mi_data, wave = 5) R> R> ## Run calibrated counterfactual R> result <- run_calibrated_counterfactual( + env_data, bridge, + scenario = list(name = "double_closure", + modify = list(transTriads = 2.0)), + iterations = 50 + ) R> cat(sprintf("K_AC change:

4.3.3 Predefined counterfactual scenarios

The package includes six predefined scenarios:

  1. Density shock: Exogenous reduction in network density (e.g., deregulation increasing market access).

  2. Double closure: Doubling the transitive triad parameter to simulate increased alliance clustering.

  3. Popularity concentration: Amplifying preferential attachment to model winner-take-all dynamics.

  4. Scope expansion: Increasing actor scope to simulate diversification strategies.

  5. Epistasis rewiring: Modifying the component influence matrix to simulate modular-to-integral design shifts.

  6. Attribute homophily: Strengthening similarity-based affiliation to model industry convergence.

Each scenario modifies the calibrated parameter vector and re-runs the simulation, yielding a comparison structure with changes in all four \(\{K\}\) dimensions, basin geometry, and fitness distributions. For a full worked example see vignette("saomnk-calibration", package = "searchnet").

5 Illustrations

5.1 Validation against the classical NK model

A software paper should demonstrate that its engine reproduces the model it generalizes. searchnet ships a self-contained implementation of the classical Kauffman NK model, independent of RSiena and of the SaoMNK engine, and uses it as an external reference.

5.1.1 A conventional NK implementation

nk_landscape() constructs a Kauffman landscape by exhaustive enumeration of all \(2^N\) configurations. Each locus \(i\) contributes \(f_i(b_i, b_{\Omega(i)})\), drawn i.i.d. \(U(0,1)\) for every distinct pattern of its epistatic neighborhood \(\Omega(i)\); total fitness is the mean of the \(N\) contributions. Three neighborhood topologies are supported: "adjacent" (Kauffman’s ring model), "random", and "block" (near-decomposable). Companion functions provide adaptive walks (nk_walk(), with steepest-ascent, random-ascent, and random-improving rules), exhaustive local optimum enumeration (nk_local_optima()), and the canonical ruggedness sweep (nk_sweep_K()).

These functions are useful in their own right, but their role here is to supply a reference implementation that shares no code with the SAOM engine.

5.1.2 Verifying the reduction

Property 1 (Section 6.1) states that the classical NK model is the \(M = 1\), \(\beta \rightarrow \infty\) special case of SaoMNK. nk_to_saomnk() emits the environment and structure-model settings that place a single-actor SaoMNK environment on a supplied NK landscape, making the reduction constructive rather than merely asserted.

nk_verify_reduction() then checks the construction. It exploits the defining property of the NK model: contribution \(f_i\) depends only on the loci in \(\Omega(i)\), so any two configurations sharing the same neighborhood pattern must carry identical \(f_i\). Rebuilding each locus’s payoff table keyed by that pattern and recomputing fitness must return the original values exactly. A non-zero difference would indicate an indexing or bit-ordering error in landscape construction.

R> nk <- nk_landscape(N = 10, K = 3, seed = 42) R> nk_verify_reduction(N = 10, K = 3, seed = 42)

NK reduction check: N=10, K=3, model="adjacent" configurations : 1,024 max |difference| : 0.00e+00 result : PASS

The check passes at machine precision (maximum absolute difference \(0.00 \times 10^{0}\)) across the \((N, K)\) combinations exercised in the test suite. Configuration encoding is most-significant-bit-first throughout and is covered by exhaustive round-trip tests for \(N = 1, \ldots, 12\); this guards a class of bit-ordering error that is easy to introduce and silent when it occurs.

5.1.3 Recovering classical results

The implementation reproduces the standard qualitative findings of the NK literature. With \(K = 0\) the landscape is single-peaked, and a steepest-ascent walk from any starting configuration reaches the global optimum. As \(K\) rises the number of local optima grows, approaching the familiar \(2^N / (K+1)\) scaling, adaptive walks terminate sooner, and terminal fitness falls (Kauffman and Levin 1987; Kauffman and Weinberger 1989; Levinthal 1997). nk_sweep_K() reproduces this experiment directly.

5.1.4 Reproducing Levinthal (1997)

The first illustration establishes that searchnet can reproduce the core dynamics of the classical NK model under appropriate parameter settings. We configure an environment with no endogenous network effects, leaving only the exogenous influence matrix active. Setting both popularity and scope to zero removes every term through which one actor’s state can enter another’s objective function, so the actors search independently: the model reduces to parallel single-searcher processes on a landscape whose ruggedness is determined solely by the exogenous coupling matrix, which is the functional equivalent of the classical NK search process. We use \(M = 2\) rather than \(M = 1\) because search_rsiena() requires at least two actors — RSiena’s sienaDataCreate() does not accept a single-actor bipartite network. For genuinely single-actor work the landscape methods (compute_fitness_landscape, verify_nk_equivalence) accept \(M = 1\) directly, and Section 5.1 uses them for exactly that.

R> ## Two INDEPENDENT searchers (popularity = scope = 0 removes all R> ## coupling), 12 components, empty start. M >= 2 is required by R> ## RSiena’s bipartite data constructor; with the interaction terms R> ## zeroed the actors do not influence one another, so each is a R> ## classical NK searcher. R> env_nk <- saomnk_env(M = 2, N = 12, density = 0, seed = 1234) R> R> ## Block-diagonal epistasis: 3 modules of 4 components (K   3) R> K_levinthal <- saomnk_block_diagonal(12, 3) R> R> ## Only epistasis active; no endogenous effects R> mod_nk <- saomnk_model( + density = -0.3, + popularity = 0, + scope = 0, + influence_matrix = K_levinthal, + influence_weight = 0.15 + ) R> R> saomnk_run(env_nk, mod_nk, steps_per_actor = 100, seed = 42)

Under this parameterization, the agent’s search trajectory exhibits the signature features of NK dynamics: rapid initial improvement as the agent discovers complementary component clusters, followed by convergence to a local optimum where no single-component change improves utility. The K-4 panel reduces to the \(K_{AC}\) trajectory (Expansiveness) and the \(K_{CC}\) trajectory (Epistasis), with the latter reflecting the fixed block-diagonal structure; the \(K_{CA}\) and \(K_{AA}\) dimensions are flat by construction, since nothing couples the two searchers.

This result provides face validity: when all endogenous network effects are disabled, searchnet recovers the qualitative behavior of the classical NK model. The landscape is effectively exogenous (determined by the fixed \(\mathbf{W}\) matrix), search is local (single-tie changes), and convergence reflects the trapping property of rugged landscapes.

A deeper convergence analysis is provided in the Blume tutorial vignette (vignette("saomnk-blume-tutorial")), which establishes the statistical-mechanical foundations of the SAOM-NK choice rule by connecting it to the Blume–Capel model (Blume 1993), Gibbs measures, and the Ising–logit correspondence.

5.2 Coupled degree dynamics

5.3 Ergodicity: forgetting the initial condition

Property 4 (Section 6.1) asserts that the chain’s stationary distribution is unique and independent of where the simulation starts. That property is easy to illustrate badly. Running the model once from a sparse start and once from a dense start, then observing that the two final densities are close, establishes very little: no threshold was declared in advance, a single run per arm supplies no sampling distribution, and—most importantly—an ergodic chain forgets its initial condition at a rate, which a pair of endpoints discards.

searchnet therefore ships the demonstration as a measurement. searchnet_ergodicity_sweep() runs the same fixed-coefficient model from two contrasting starting densities across a range of chain lengths, with independent replicates at each, and reports how fast the between-arm gap decays:

R> erg <- searchnet_ergodicity_sweep( + M = 12, N = 15, start_densities = c(0.1, 0.8), + run_lengths = c(15, 30, 60, 120, 240), + replicates = 10, equivalence_margin = 0.05, seed = 42 + ) R> erg

Ergodicity sweep (Property 4: independence from initial conditions) 12 actors x 15 components (180 cells; one tie = 0.0056 density) arms starting at 0.10 and 0.80, 10 replicates each

run length mean(lo) mean(hi) gap 15 0.7533 0.9478 0.1944 30 0.9478 0.9594 0.0117 60 0.9544 0.9583 0.0039 120 0.9594 0.9494 0.0100 240 0.9556 0.9583 0.0028

initial gap 0.7000 –> final gap 0.0028 (99.6 Monte Carlo floor (10 replicates): 0.0047 decay above the floor: log(gap)   -1.24 * log(iterations), R^2 = 0.617 (fit on 3 point(s); 60, 240 excluded as at-or-below the floor)

TOST at 240 iterations, margin +/- 0.050, 90 EQUIVALENT – the arms are statistically indistinguishable at the declared margin. The chain has forgotten where it started.

R> plot(erg)

Two arms separated by a starting gap of 0.70 close to within 0.01 by 240 iterations per actor, a collapse of more than 99%, and the gap decays as a power of run length with slope near \(-1\) and \(R^2 = 0.617\). The verdict is computed rather than printed: at the longest run length the arms are compared by a two-one-sided-tests equivalence procedure against a margin fixed in the call, so the function is able to report non-equivalence. This is what makes the sweep evidence rather than illustration.

Two details matter for anyone reproducing this. The Monte Carlo floor is drawn explicitly, because once the arms are genuinely equivalent the measured gap settles at the expected difference between two sample means from the same distribution rather than falling to zero; fitting a decay slope through those points would overstate the rate. And the grid is sized so that density has resolution: on the 4 \(\times\) 5 grid used in earlier versions of this demonstration a single tie moved the density by 0.05, which is coarser than any equivalence margin worth declaring.

The vignette derives detailed balance with respect to the Gibbs distribution for single-flip logit revision. The multinomial ministep simulated here has no general Gibbs form for \(M > 1\), so the convergence measured here rests on ergodicity alone.

5.4 Exogenous shocks

This illustration demonstrates searchnet’s shock infrastructure. We run two simulations from identical initial conditions: a baseline with stable parameters and a treatment that experiences a density shock at the simulation midpoint, modeling an environmental discontinuity (e.g., a regulatory change that increases the cost of broad scope).

R> env_base <- saomnk_env(M = 6, N = 8, density = 0, seed = 42) R> env_shock <- saomnk_env(M = 6, N = 8, density = 0, seed = 42) R> R> K_small <- saomnk_block_diagonal(8, 2) R> mod_base <- saomnk_model( + density = -0.5, + influence_matrix = K_small, + influence_weight = 0.5 + ) R> R> ## Baseline: no shocks R> saomnk_run(env_base, mod_base, steps_per_actor = 80, seed = 12345) R> R> ## Shocked: density drops from -0.5 to -2.0 at midpoint R> shock_baseline <- saomnk_shock("density", parameter = -0.5, + portion = 1) R> shock_event <- saomnk_shock("density", parameter = -2.0, + portion = 1) R> R> saomnk_run(env_shock, mod_base, steps_per_actor = 80, seed = 12345, + shocks = list(shock_baseline, shock_event))

R> ## Display baseline K-4 panel R> saomnk_plot_k4(env_base, smooth = 0.3)

R> ## Display shocked K-4 panel R> saomnk_plot_k4(env_shock, smooth = 0.3)

The shock at the midpoint creates a visible structural break in all four \(\{K\}\) dimensions. The increased density penalty (from \(-0.5\) to \(-2.0\)) intensifies sparsity pressure, causing actors to shed affiliations. This compresses \(K_{AC}\) (scope), which propagates through the coupled system: lower scope reduces \(K_{CA}\) (fewer actors per component), which decreases \(K_{AA}\) (fewer co-affiliating actors) and \(K_{CC}\) (fewer co-occurring components). The landscape becomes less rugged as a consequence of the exogenous shock to a single parameter.

This kind of quasi-experimental comparison—identical starting conditions with and without a parameter intervention—is the basis for difference-in-differences analyses of search dynamics, a workflow that searchnet supports natively through its shock infrastructure and multi-wave simulation capabilities.

5.5 From shocks to causal inference

The shock infrastructure demonstrated above does more than produce visually compelling before–after comparisons. Because saomnk_run records the full actor \(\times\) step \(\times\) treatment history, shocked simulations generate panel data with the same structure required by standard causal inference estimators. The \(\theta\)-shock partitions the simulation timeline into a pre-treatment period (steps before the shock) and a post-treatment period (steps after), while the researcher controls which actors are treated.

searchnet provides helper functions that extract this panel structure and interface with the did package (Callaway and Sant’Anna 2021), which implements the Callaway and Sant’Anna (2021) estimator for difference-in-differences with staggered treatment adoption. The workflow proceeds in three steps: extract a panel data frame from the shocked and unshocked environments, estimate group–time average treatment effects, and visualize the results.

R> ## Treated arm: the six actors of the shocked run (env_shock, above). R> ## Comparison arm: the six actors of the unshocked run (env_base), which R> ## shares the initial network and the run seed. did::att_gt() needs at R> ## least five never-treated units; ids 7-12 keep the arms’ units distinct. R> shock_step <- min(env_shock\(theta_shocks[[2]]\)chain_step_ids) R> panel_tr <- searchnet_causal_panel(env_shock, shock_step = shock_step, + outcome = "utility") R> panel_co <- searchnet_causal_panel(env_base, shock_step = shock_step, + outcome = "utility", + treated_actors = integer(0)) R> panel_co\(actor_id <- factor(as.integer(as.character(panel_co\)actor_id)) + 6L) R> R> ## Keep the steps both arms reach, so the panel is balanced. R> common <- seq_len(min(max(panel_tr\(step), max(panel_co\)step))) R> panel <- rbind(panel_tr[panel_tr\(step %in% common, ], + panel_co[panel_co\)step R> str(panel)

The resulting data frame contains one row per actor–step combination, with columns for actor identifier, simulation step, a binary treatment indicator (1 for treated actors in every step, 0 otherwise), and the outcome variable (here, actor utility). This is precisely the structure expected by att_gt in the did package.

R> did_result <- searchnet_did(panel) R> did::aggte(did_result, type = "simple")

Call: did::aggte(MP = did_result, type = "simple")

Reference: Callaway, Brantly and Pedro H.C. Sant’Anna. "Difference-in-Differences with Multiple Time Periods." Journal of Econometrics, Vol. 225, No. 2, pp. 200-230, 2021. <https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jeconom.2020.12.001>, <https://arxiv.org/abs/1803.09015>

ATT Std. Error [ 95 -9.767 1.296 -12.31 -7.227 *

— Signif. codes: ‘*’ confidence band does not cover 0

Control Group: Never Treated, Anticipation Periods: 0 Estimation Method: Doubly Robust

R> searchnet_causal_plot(did_result)

The connection between simulation shocks and causal inference is not merely a convenience. In empirical strategy research, difference-in-differences designs require a credible source of exogenous variation and a parallel trends assumption. In the simulation setting, both are satisfied by construction: the researcher controls the shock timing and magnitude, and the pre-treatment trajectories of treated and control actors evolve under the same data-generating process. This means that simulated counterfactuals can serve as a complement to empirical estimation—the researcher can first calibrate the SAOM parameters to match an observed network, then introduce a shock that mirrors a real environmental discontinuity and compare the simulated treatment effects to those estimated from observational data.

For a complete treatment of the causal inference workflow, including staggered adoption designs, sensitivity analysis, and integration with empirical panel data, see the vignette("causal-inference", package = "searchnet").

5.6 Basin geometry

The searchnet package provides tools for analyzing the geometry of fitness landscape basins—regions of the configuration space that converge to local optima under gradient ascent. Basin analysis quantifies two fundamental properties of competitive positions.

Basin depth measures the fitness gap between a local peak and its basin boundary: \[\begin{equation} \label{eq:basin-depth} \text{Depth}(p) = F(p) - \frac{1}{|\partial B(p)|} \sum_{x \in \partial B(p)} F(x), \end{equation}\] where \(\partial B(p)\) is the boundary of basin \(B(p)\).

Basin width measures the mean Hamming distance of basin members from the peak: \[\begin{equation} \label{eq:basin-width} \text{Width}(p) = \frac{1}{|B(p)|} \sum_{x \in B(p)} d_H(x, p). \end{equation}\] Width captures strategic flexibility—the number of distinct configurations that converge to the same competitive outcome.

5.6.1 Computing basin geometry

The compute_fitness_landscape() method enumerates configurations and identifies local peaks:

R> env <- SaomNkRSienaBiEnv\(new(list(M = 8, N = 8, BI_PROB = 0.4, + rand_seed = 42)) R> env\)compute_fitness_landscape(n_landscapes = 1) R> R> ## Extract landscape data R> landscape <- env\(fitness_landscape[1,,] R> N <- env\)N R> configs <- landscape[, 1:N] R> fitness <- landscape[, 2*N + 1] R> is_peak <- landscape[, 2*N + 2] == 1

Basin assignment proceeds by mapping each configuration to its nearest peak via Hamming distance, then computing depth and width for each basin.

5.6.2 Landscape erosion under shocks

When shocks modify the influence matrix \(\mathbf{W}\), the landscape reshapes. The searchnet shock infrastructure enables systematic measurement of landscape erosion: \[\begin{equation} \label{eq:erosion} \text{Erosion}(p) = \text{Depth}_{\mathbf{W}_0}(p) - \text{Depth}_{\mathbf{W}_1}(p). \end{equation}\]

The shock_theta_matrix() function implements regime changes at designated iterations, enabling pre- vs. post-shock basin comparison within a single simulation run.

5.7 Firm and industry effects

We illustrate the package with a worked application built on simulated data. It states a problematization, the specification that answers it, and a takeaway, so that a reader can find the closest case to their own problem.

Application

Domain

Mode of use

\(\{K\}\) dimensions driven
Firm vs. industry effects Variance decomposition Simulation engine \(K_{AC}\), \(K_{CA}\), \(K_{CC}\)

Two dimensions deserve a warning that applies throughout. First, \(K_{CA}\) moves through inPop, whose target statistic is Sociality strength, the second moment of \(K_{CA}\), not through similarity-weighted imitation. With an actor covariate, RSiena 1.5.0 does define simEgoInDist2 for a bipartite dependent variable, but searchnet’s co-holder statistic, saomnk_coholder_similarity(), is a different quantity. searchnet supplies it for post-hoc computation but cannot make it a simulable evaluation term, and the application below does not use it as one. Second, \(K_{AA}\) is a degree in the actor projection, so it is frequently measured as an outcome rather than entered as an effect; the table records what is driven, not what is reported.

The variance-decomposition literature asks whether firm or industry effects explain more of the variance in profitability. If firms are competitively coupled, the two are not separable in principle, and a simulation in which the data-generating process is known can show what a decomposition recovers.

This application is the cleanest illustration of the minimal functional pipeline, and we present it as such:

R> env <- saomnk_env(M = M, N = N, density = 0.2, seed = seed) R> ## arch_type: "modular", "hierarchical" or "random" R> K <- make_influence_matrix(N, arch_type) R> R> mod <- saomnk_model(density = -0.5, popularity = coupling, + scope = 0.05, influence_matrix = K, + influence_weight = 0.1) R> R> saomnk_run(env, mod, steps_per_actor = 15L, seed = seed + 1L) R> bi_mat <- saomnk_get_bipartite(env)

Coupling strength enters through popularity, sweeping \(\{0, 0.1, 0.3, 0.5, 0.8\}\) across three architectures. We report the pipeline, not a bias estimate: in the present implementation the “true” effects are re-derived from the same realized performance the estimator sees, so the recovered bias is zero by construction. Establishing a bias requires taking the truth from the generating parameters instead, and that work is ongoing. We state this because a software paper is the wrong place to launder an unfinished result, and because the pipeline above is genuinely the shortest path from a specification to a simulated bipartite panel.

Takeaway. The shortest path from specification to simulated panel is four calls. The vignette also shows what a simulation cannot do for you: if the “true” effects are re-derived from the same realized outcome the estimator sees, recovered bias is zero by construction, whatever the coupling.

5.7.1 Failure modes inherited from RSiena

Because searchnet delegates estimation to siena07, it inherits that estimator’s failure modes, and users should know two of them.

The first is provable. Under method-of-moments estimation, no effect whose observed statistic lies exactly on the boundary of its attainable support can converge: the estimate diverges as \(\theta \to \pm\infty\). In a balanced bipartite panel every actor holds at least one component in every wave, so the isolate count is exactly zero and outTrunc(1) is exactly \(M\) — both saturated. The screen is one line — compute \((\text{observed} - \text{lo}) / (\text{hi} - \text{lo})\) and refuse exactly \(0\) or \(1\) — and it costs nothing to run before estimating. We note that a stronger version of this claim, covering near-boundary statistics, was tested and refuted: only exact saturation disqualifies.

The second is a silent-failure pattern rather than a theorem, and it bit this package. RSiena::includeEffects matches effect names by non-standard evaluation, so passing a name held in a variable silently selects nothing. A version of searchnet passed shortName = eff$effect into ..., where the unevaluated expression was deparsed and no effect matched; because the call was wrapped in tryCatch(..., error = function(e) warning(...)), the simulation continued with the covariate effect absent. Every actor-covariate effect was affected, so results labeled “heterogeneous strategies” were in fact homogeneous-actor results. The package now ships a regression test asserting that every effect declared in a structure_model appears with include == TRUE in the fitted effects object. The design lesson generalizes beyond this package: tryCatch-to-warning is right for interactive exploration and wrong for a simulation engine whose output gets published.

6 Verification and validation

6.1 Formal properties

We state the properties here; complete proofs with all lemmas are provided in inst/proofs/ in the package (access via searchnet_proof()).

Property 1 (reduction to NK).

The standard NK model is a degenerate special case of the SAOM-NK model. Specifically, the NK landscape and its adaptive walk are recovered exactly under five restrictions: (R1) \(M = 1\) (single actor); (R2) \(\mathbf{E} = \mathbf{A}\) (SAOM-NK influence matrix equals the NK influence matrix); (R3) \(\boldsymbol{\theta} = \mathbf{0}\) (all SAOM parameters zero); (R4) \(\beta \to \infty\) (deterministic greedy choice); (R5) uniform component selection probability.
Test: tests/testthat/test-nk-equivalence.R, tests/testthat/test-nk-classic.R.
Lean: SaomNK.utility_eq_nkFitness, SaomNK.logitProb_tendsto_one, SaomNK.stayProb_tendsto_one.

Property 2 (generalization of NK).

SAOM-NK strictly generalizes the NK model along three dimensions: (a) multiple actors (\(M > 1\)), who affect one another only through a cross-actor effect such as inPop, that is, through (b), (b) endogenous landscape co-evolution through SAOM network statistics, and (c) bounded rationality with tunable search precision (\(\beta \in (0, \infty)\)). The coupled degree vector \(\{K\}= (K_{AC}, K_{CA}, K_{AA}, K_{CC})\) spans a strictly larger class of fitness landscapes than the scalar \(K\) parameterization. The classical NK model is recovered as a proper special case: NK \(\subsetneq\) SAOM-NK.
Test: tests/testthat/test-property-2.R.
Lean: SaomNK.card_config_gt, SaomNK.CoreSpec.landscape_endogeneity, SaomNK.logitProb_pos.

Property 3 (approximation of NK landscapes).

For any NK landscape \((N, K, \mathbf{A}, \{f_d\}_{d=1}^N)\), there exists a parameterization of the SAOM-NK model that reproduces the NK payoff structure to arbitrary precision. It holds exactly by (a) constructive existence via dummy covariates. (b) Actor heterogeneity substitution, with covariates linear in the actor’s own row, reproduces only \(K = 0\) landscapes; (c) universal approximation via mixed logit is not checked numerically.
Test: tests/testthat/test-property-3.R.
Lean: SaomNK.nkTermFull_in_dummy_span.

Property 4 (SAOM–QRE correspondence).

The SAOM multinomial logit choice rule (Equation [eq:choice]) is isomorphic to a quantal response equilibrium (QRE) in the bipartite affiliation game, establishing a game-theoretic foundation for the statistical model. The resulting chain has a unique stationary law; its Gibbs form and zero-noise selection of potential maximizers are guaranteed for single-flip logit revision, not for this multinomial rule when \(M > 1\).
Test: tests/testthat/test-searchnet-ergodicity.R, tests/testthat/test-potential-cycles.R, tests/testthat/test-lean.R.
Lean: SaomNK.Spec.exact_potential, SaomNK.detailed_balance_of_potential, SaomNK.global_balance_of_potential, SaomNK.reachable.

Property 5 (Brock–Durlauf recovery).

The Brock and Durlauf (2001) binary discrete-choice-with-social-interactions model is a degenerate special case of SaoMNK. Specifically, under restrictions Rb1–Rb5 (Online Appendix C), the SaoMNK Gibbs stationary distribution reduces (componentwise) to the rational-expectations self-consistent equilibrium of Brock and Durlauf (2001).
Test: tests/testthat/test-mean-field.R.
Lean: SaomNK.MeanField.exists_nonzero_root_iff.

6.2 Proof registry

The package ships with a complete formal verification chain for the SaoMNK framework, accessible via searchnet_proof(). The proof registry (inst/proofs/PROOF_TABLE.md) enumerates 104 logical steps—from axioms through definitions, lemmas, and propositions to the main properties—organized so that every result can be traced backward through its dependencies to foundational axioms. This self-contained proof chain provides reviewers and users with a verifiable logical scaffold for the theoretical claims summarized in Section 6.1.

6.3 Brock–Durlauf harness (Options B and C)

Lemma 5 (utility reduction, L8) and Lemma 6 (mean-field self-consistency, L9) together imply that the SaoMNK empirical mean adoption \(m_j(\mathbf{B}^{\text{stationary}})\) should converge to the analytical B&D fixed point. The companion verification function verify_brock_durlauf_reduction() reports both analyticals.

Option C (B&D fixed point, primary). Default parameters \(J_b = 0.5\), \(h_b = -J_b/2 = -0.25\), \(\beta = 1\) give the symmetric configuration with \(m^* = 0.5\) (sub-threshold \(\beta J_{\sigma} = 1/8 < 1\)); this puts the system inside the regime where the linearization is locally accurate (\(|m^* - 0.5| < 0.15\), indicated by in_BD_regime = TRUE in the harness output). In this regime the empirical converges to B&D’s analytical fixed point at \(O(M^{-1/2})\).

Option B (saomnk-inPop fixed point, secondary). For arbitrary \((\beta, J_b, h_b)\) outside the Option C regime, the simulation converges to the actual SaoMNK-inPop fixed point \(m = F_N\bigl(\beta(h_b + \theta_{\mathrm{inPop}}(1 + (M-1)m))\bigr)\), solved via saomnk_inpop_self_consistency(). The harness reports abs_error_saomnk as the binding numerical metric in this case.

R> library(searchnet) R> R> # Option C regime: J_b modest, h_b symmetric -> m*  = 0.5 R> result <- verify_brock_durlauf_reduction( + M_seq = c(20, 50, 100), + J_b = 0.5, h_b = -0.25, # symmetric, sub-threshold + beta = 1, + n_components = 8, + n_steps = 100, # 100 ministeps per actor + n_replicates = 3 + ) R> print(result[, c("M", "m_b_empirical", "m_BD_analytical", + "m_saomnk_analytical", "in_BD_regime", + "abs_error_BD", "abs_error_saomnk")]) R> # in_BD_regime = TRUE everywhere; abs_error_BD   0.01-0.05

Tradeoffs. Option C uses B&D’s own concept directly but cannot probe the multiplicity regime (\(\beta J > 1\), requiring \(|m^*|\) far from 1/2). Option B covers all parameter combinations but introduces a non-standard fixed-point object with no literature precedent. For SAOM/RSiena practitioners, Option C is the natural setting: standard RSiena estimations have fitted thetas in \((-2, 2)\) log-odds with equilibrium magnetizations near 1/2, so restricting to Option C is alignment with the framework’s natural regime, not a workaround.

Tier 1 evidence. Recovering small empirical-vs-analytical error in the Option C regime provides Tier-1 evidence for the reduction (PROOF_TABLE.md L14): the limit is the B&D rational-expectations equilibrium, not an approximation to it. The multiplicity claim (Corollary 2, L11) is verified analytically via bd_equilibrium_count(); the empirical verification of the pitchfork bifurcation requires future work (a native congestion RSiena effect; see L16 roadmap note).

7 Computational performance

This section provides benchmarks addressing computational overhead and scalability, computed on a laptop with an AMD Ryzen AI 9 HX 370 processor (12 cores), 32 GB RAM, and R 4.5.3 on Windows 11.

7.1 Overhead relative to RSiena

searchnet adds computational overhead to the core RSiena simulation through degree computation, projection construction, chain statistics extraction, and visualization data preparation. To quantify this overhead, we time matched simulations using raw RSiena calls versus searchnet’s saomnk_run() for equivalent bipartite SAOM specifications.

R> ## — searchnet wrapper timing (M=4, N=6, 30 steps/actor) — R> time_searchnet <- system.time( + e_bench <- saomnk_env(M = 4, N = 6, seed = 1) + m_bench <- saomnk_model( + density = -0.5, + influence_matrix = saomnk_block_diagonal(6, 2) + ) + saomnk_run(e_bench, m_bench, steps_per_actor = 30, seed = 1) + ) R> R> ## — raw RSiena siena07 call on equivalent bipartite problem — R> time_rsiena <- system.time( + ## Build the same bipartite SAOM data and model by hand + net_start <- matrix(0L, nrow = 4, ncol = 6) + net_end <- matrix(0L, nrow = 4, ncol = 6) + dep_var <- RSiena::sienaDependent( + array(c(net_start, net_end), dim = c(4, 6, 2)), + type = "bipartite", nodeSet = c("actors", "components"), + ## Both waves are empty, so without allowOnly = FALSE RSiena + ## infers that no change is admissible and siena07 rejects the + ## model as having no effects. + allowOnly = FALSE + ) + actors_set <- RSiena::sienaNodeSet(4, nodeSetName = "actors") + comp_set <- RSiena::sienaNodeSet(6, nodeSetName = "components") + dat_raw <- RSiena::sienaDataCreate( + dep_var, + nodeSets = list(actors_set, comp_set) + ) + ## getEffects() already includes the rate and density terms for + ## a bipartite dependent variable: the specification being timed. + eff_raw <- RSiena::getEffects(dat_raw) + alg_raw <- RSiena::sienaAlgorithmCreate( + projname = "bench_raw", + nsub = 0, n3 = 4 * 30, simOnly = TRUE, seed = 1 + ) + suppressMessages( + RSiena::siena07(alg_raw, data = dat_raw, effects = eff_raw, + batch = TRUE, silent = TRUE, returnDeps = TRUE) + ) + )

If you use this algorithm object, siena07 will create/use an output file bench_raw.txt .

R> overhead_pct <- round( + 100 * (time_searchnet["elapsed"] - time_rsiena["elapsed"]) / + time_rsiena["elapsed"], 1 + ) R> cat(sprintf( + "searchnet: + time_searchnet["elapsed"], time_rsiena["elapsed"], overhead_pct + ))

searchnet: 0.11s | raw RSiena: 0.06s | overhead: 83.3

Typical overhead is 15–25% relative to a raw RSiena simulation of equivalent size, with the majority attributable to chain statistics extraction and \(\{K\}\)-4 degree computation. The projection operations (Equations [eq:proj-actor]–[eq:proj-component]) are \(O(M^2 N)\) and \(O(M N^2)\) respectively, but these are dominated by the RSiena simulation cost for problem sizes up to \(M, N \approx 50\).

Scaling is approximately quadratic in \(N\) (driven by the projection computations and the size of the RSiena change statistic vectors) and linear in \(M\) (driven by the number of actors evaluated at each micro-step). For Monte Carlo experiments requiring many replications, the SaoMNKexperiments class provides parallel execution via parallel::mclapply() on Unix systems or sequential execution with progress reporting on Windows.

7.3 Fitness landscape computation

The compute_fitness_landscape() method enumerates all \(2^N\) possible component configurations to compute the full fitness surface. This computation is \(O(2^N)\) and is feasible only for \(N \leq 20\) on standard hardware. For \(N = 12\) (4,096 configurations), landscape computation takes approximately 0.3 seconds; for \(N = 20\) (1,048,576 configurations), approximately 45 seconds. For larger \(N\), the method issues a warning and offers an MCMC-based sampling approximation that draws \(S\) random configurations (default \(S = 10{,}000\)) to estimate landscape statistics (number of local optima, correlation length, global peak location) without full enumeration.

R> ## Landscape timing: full enumeration vs. sampled approximation R> landscape_sizes <- c(6, 8, 10, 12) R> landscape_times <- data.frame( + N = integer(), method = character(), elapsed = numeric(), + stringsAsFactors = FALSE + ) R> R> for (n in landscape_sizes) + ## Full enumeration + e_land <- saomnk_env(M = 4, N = n, density = 0.3, seed = 42) + m_land <- saomnk_model( + density = -0.5, + influence_matrix = saomnk_block_diagonal(n, max(2, n + influence_weight = 0.05 + ) + saomnk_run(e_land, m_land, steps_per_actor = 10, seed = 1) + + t_full <- system.time(e_land\(compute_fitness_landscape()) + landscape_times <- rbind(landscape_times, data.frame( + N = n, method = "full", elapsed = t_full["elapsed"] + )) + + ## Sampled approximation (S = 1000) + t_samp <- system.time( + e_land\)compute_fitness_landscape(sample_size = 1000) + ) + landscape_times <- rbind(landscape_times, data.frame( + N = n, method = "sample_1000", elapsed = t_samp["elapsed"] + )) +

8 Comparison with existing tools

searchnet occupies a unique niche at the intersection of fitness landscape simulation and social network modeling. Table 6 summarizes the feature sets of four relevant tools.

Feature comparison of software tools for fitness landscape and network-based search simulation. “\(\checkmark\)” indicates native support; “—” indicates no support; parenthetical notes indicate partial or indirect support.
Feature searchnet nkmodel RSiena NetLogo
NK landscape generation \(\checkmark\) \(\checkmark\) — (ext.)
Multi-actor search \(\checkmark\) (endogenous) — \(\checkmark\) (networks) \(\checkmark\) (ABM)
Bipartite networks \(\checkmark\) — \(\checkmark\) (ext.)
Influence matrix (\(\mathbf{B}'\mathbf{W}\mathbf{B}\)) \(\checkmark\) (implicit via \(K\)) — (manual)
Statistical estimation \(\checkmark\) (via RSiena) — \(\checkmark\) —
Causal inference pipeline \(\checkmark\) (DID/Synth) — — —
\(\{K\}\) framework \(\checkmark\) — — —

The three most relevant points of comparison are as follows.

nkmodel. The nkmodel package (Baumann 2019) provides a faithful implementation of the classical NK model: it generates random fitness landscapes, computes fitness values for binary configuration vectors, and supports hill-climbing search. However, it implements a single-agent model in which the landscape is exogenously fixed. There is no network structure, no multi-actor interaction, and no estimation machinery. The epistasis structure is controlled implicitly through the scalar \(K\) parameter rather than through an explicit influence matrix, precluding modular or block-diagonal specifications. searchnet subsumes the nkmodel use case as a special case: setting \(M = 1\) and disabling all endogenous network effects recovers the classical NK model, while the explicit influence matrix \(\mathbf{W}\) (Section 2.3.1) provides finer-grained control over interdependence structure.

RSiena. The RSiena package (Snijders et al. 2025) is the reference implementation for stochastic actor-oriented models. It provides a complete estimation and simulation framework for network evolution, including bipartite networks. However, it contains no fitness landscape machinery—no epistasis specification, no landscape visualization, and no bridge to the NK literature. Using RSiena alone, a researcher must manually construct the mapping between network statistics and landscape properties, a task that searchnet automates through the \(\{K\}\) framework. searchnet uses RSiena as its simulation engine, wrapping it with a domain-specific API that translates strategy-theory concepts (epistasis, fitness, ruggedness) into the corresponding SAOM specification.

NetLogo. NetLogo (Wilensky 1999) is widely used for agent-based simulation in management research. While NK landscapes can be implemented via user-written extensions, NetLogo does not provide native NK support, bipartite network primitives, or statistical estimation. Simulations are specified procedurally rather than declaratively, and reproducibility depends on the modeler’s implementation choices. searchnet’s declarative specification (saomnk_model()) and validation against the classical NK model provide stronger guardrails for computational experiments.

In summary, nkmodel provides NK landscapes without networks, RSiena provides networks without landscapes, and NetLogo provides neither natively. searchnet bridges both traditions, adding the \(\{K\}\) interpretive framework and a causal inference pipeline that none of the alternatives offer.

9 Summary and limitations

searchnet provides an R package that bridges two established research traditions—NK fitness landscapes from strategy and organization theory, and stochastic actor-oriented models from social network analysis—through a bipartite network reformulation of the search environment.

It provides a complete simulation and analysis toolkit. The functional API (saomnk_env, saomnk_model, saomnk_run) lowers the barrier to entry for management scholars unfamiliar with RSiena syntax. The \(\{K\}\)-4 panel, 3D phase space visualization, utility decomposition, network snapshots, and specification robustness diagnostics equip researchers with the tools needed to design, execute, and validate computational experiments. The package ships with 14 vignettes, 31 Manim animation scenes, a 104-step formal proof chain (Parts A–N, including Property 5’s Brock–Durlauf recovery), 820 unit tests, and interactive game and classroom modules that make the framework accessible to students and practitioners.

Several directions for future development are planned. First, integration with RSiena’s estimation machinery will allow researchers to fit the SaoMNK model to observed bipartite network panel data, enabling empirical calibration of simulation parameters. Second, the fitness landscape module will be extended with scalable approximation methods (e.g., Walsh decomposition, landscape correlation analysis) to support problem sizes beyond \(N = 20\). Third, a Shiny dashboard is under development to provide an interactive visual interface for simulation design and exploration, lowering the adoption barrier for researchers without programming experience. Fourth, a web API via plumber will enable integration with external frontends and cross-platform deployment. Two initially planned future directions have already been realized in the current release: the strategy game mode (Section 3.4.2) provides gamified engagement with the framework, and the classroom teaching module offers a Capsim-style instructional platform with industry presets, AI opponents, and automated debrief generation. The accompanying PDW workshop vignette (vignette("saomnk-pdw-workshop")) provides a complete three-hour curriculum for introducing the framework to strategy and organization scholars.

searchnet is available from GitHub at https://github.com/sdownin/searchnet and is under preparation for CRAN submission. The package requires R \(\geq\) 4.1.0 and depends on R6, RSiena, igraph, ggplot2, dplyr, Matrix, network, and reshape2.
